draft.title: Market research and feasibility
card: new information a business collects itself for its own purpose, such as a survey, interview, focus group or trial product.
information that already exists and was collected by someone else, such as government statistics, industry reports or a competitor's website.
Research tests whether customers want the idea. A feasibility study then asks whether the idea can work and make a profit, using the costs, prices and likely sales the research suggests.
A first feasibility study is done early, before much money is spent. If the numbers do not work, the owner can change the idea or stop at a small cost.
draft.remember: Research tests what customers want. A feasibility study tests whether the idea can work and make money, before big spending.

a.q: Sam is planning a food truck in Geelong. He hands out a short questionnaire to office workers about what lunches they would buy. What type of research is this?
opts: Primary research, because he collects the data himself
Secondary research, because office workers already know
Primary research, because it uses data from a report
Secondary research, because the questions are short
a.why: Sam collects new information himself for his own purpose, so it is primary research. Secondary research uses information someone else has already collected, such as a published report.
a.clue: Who collected the information, and was it new?

b.q: Priya wants to open a bike repair shop in Bendigo. Before signing a lease, she compares expected repair prices, rent and wages with the number of repairs she could expect. Why is this useful?
opts: It shows whether the idea could make a profit early on
It proves customers will remain loyal to her shop for years
It replaces the need to collect any market research
It guarantees the shop will earn a profit once it opens
b.why: A first feasibility study checks whether the costs and likely sales could make a profit, before much money is spent. It does not guarantee success or prove loyalty, and it relies on research rather than replacing it.
b.clue: The study is done early, and it tests the numbers rather than promising results.

a.best: Primary research, because he collects the data himself

b.best: It shows whether the idea could make a profit early on

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('could'), while every distractor uses an absolute ('guarantees', 'proves', 'replaces the need'). A student can pick it by test-taking logic alone.
The clue gives the answer away. 'The study is done early' echoes 'early on' in the right option, and 'rather than promising results' rules out the 'guarantees' and 'proves' distractors.

'Make a profit early on' is ambiguous. It can read as the shop making a profit soon after opening, rather than the check being done early. Better: 'It shows, before she spends much, whether the idea could make a profit'.

a.q: Sam is planning a food truck in Geelong. He hands out a short questionnaire to office workers about what lunches they would buy. What type of research is this?
opts: Primary research, because he collects the data himself
Secondary research, because office workers already know
Primary research, because it uses data from a report

b.q: Priya wants to open a bike repair shop in Bendigo. Before signing a lease, she compares expected repair prices, rent and wages with the number of repairs she could expect. What does this comparison do?
opts: It tests, before big spending, whether the shop could profit
It tests, after the shop opens, how much profit it has made
It tests whether customers want the shop, with no research
It tests, as secondary research, what other shops charge
b.why: Weighing likely prices and sales against costs is a first feasibility study, done before much money is spent to see if the idea could make a profit. It does not replace research: it uses the likely sales and prices that research suggests, and research is what tests whether customers want the idea.
b.clue: Think about what Priya is weighing up, and when she does it.
